plan.prompt: Add a notifications feature as three independent workstreams that can be built in parallel by different engineers, with no dependencies between the streams: (1) a notifications database table plus its migration, (2) a REST API with send and list endpoints, and (3) a settings UI panel to toggle notification types. Emphasize that the three lanes are independent.

nodes.title: Notifications table migration
nodes.summary: Create the notifications database table with id, sender_id, recipient_id, notification_type, content, read_status, and timestamps. Purely backend; independent of API and UI lanes.

nodes.title: Notifications migration test
nodes.summary: Verify the notifications table migration applies and rolls back, and that the schema columns match the expected contract.

nodes.title: Notifications REST API (send + list)
nodes.summary: Expose POST /notifications/send to store a notification and GET /notifications to list notifications for a user with pagination/filtering. Independent API lane.

nodes.title: Notifications API test
nodes.summary: Cover the send and list endpoints: payload validation, persistence on send, and pagination/filtering on list.

nodes.title: Notification settings UI panel
nodes.summary: Settings panel allowing users to toggle notification types on/off, managing user preferences. Independent UI lane focused solely on preference management.

nodes.title: Notification settings UI test
nodes.summary: Verify the settings panel renders notification type toggles and emits preference changes correctly.

assumptions.text: A notifications table migration with both up (apply) and down (rollback) paths exists for this test to exercise.
The test asserts a specific column contract (names/types) for the notifications table, since schema_keys are not enumerated in the touch-set.
The test runs against a real or ephemeral database harness capable of applying and reverting migrations.

analysis.text: Rollback may not fully restore the prior state (e.g. leftover indexes or sequences), so a passing up-migration with a partial down-migration could still pass naively without asserting clean teardown.
Test may leave the database in a dirty state if it fails between apply and rollback, polluting subsequent test runs unless wrapped in proper setup/teardown.
The expected schema contract is not pinned in the touch-set (schema_keys empty); the assertion list could drift from the actual migration without detection.
Spinning up a DB and running real migrations per test invocation can be slow; without a shared fixture this adds CI latency.

benefits.text: Provides regression protection that the notifications migration both applies and reverses cleanly, guarding against irreversible schema changes.
Pins the notifications schema column contract so unintended column drift is caught at test time.

notable_symbols.why_notable: The sole test entry point that drives the migration apply/rollback and asserts the column contract; reviewers must confirm it covers both directions and verifies teardown cleanliness.

assumptions.text: The send endpoint persists a notification record on success, which the test asserts after issuing a send request.
The list endpoint supports pagination and filtering query parameters that the test exercises.
Tests run against a test database or in-memory store that is seeded/reset between cases so persistence and pagination assertions are deterministic.

analysis.text: Payload validation tests may not cover all invalid shapes (missing recipient, empty body, oversized payload), leaving validation gaps unverified.
Persistence assertions on send depend on shared DB/store state; without per-test cleanup, leftover rows can cause pagination/filtering assertions to flake.
Pagination boundary conditions (empty page, last page, page beyond range, default page size) may be under-tested, allowing off-by-one regressions to pass.
Filtering tests that seed large datasets to verify pagination can slow the suite if not bounded to minimal fixtures.

benefits.text: Establishes regression coverage for both send and list endpoints, catching payload-validation and pagination/filtering breakages before release.
Asserts persistence-on-send, documenting the expected side effect of the send endpoint as executable behavior.

assumptions.text: NotificationSettingsPanel renders a list of NotificationTypeToggle children, one per notification type, and owns the source of preference state.
NotificationTypeToggle is a controlled component receiving a boolean value and an onChange callback rather than managing its own internal state.
This is an independent UI-only lane; no backend persistence endpoint or schema is part of this node's touch-set, so saving preferences is assumed handled elsewhere.

analysis.text: If the panel mounts before preferences load, toggles may render in an indeterminate or default-off state and silently overwrite real preferences on first interaction. No loading/empty state is evident in the touch-set.
Rapid toggling could fire overlapping persistence/onChange calls; without debounce or optimistic-state reconciliation the UI may flicker or land on a stale value if persistence is async.
A toggle save failure (network/error) is not represented in the touch-set; the toggle could appear flipped while the underlying preference never persisted, misleading the user.
Notification type labels/keys rendered from data should be treated as trusted; if any label is user- or server-supplied it must be escaped to avoid injection in the toggle row.

benefits.text: Isolating preference management into a dedicated panel and reusable toggle component keeps notification settings self-contained and testable without coupling to other settings lanes.
NotificationTypeToggle as a single reusable control lets new notification types be added by data alone, reducing per-type UI duplication.

notable_symbols.why_notable: Top-level panel that holds preference state and orchestrates the toggle list; primary surface a reviewer must inspect.
Reusable per-type control receiving value/onChange from the panel; correctness of controlled-component contract lives here.

assumptions.text: The notifications table is being created fresh with no prior version, so this is a forward-only create with no existing data to backfill.
sender_id and recipient_id are foreign keys referencing a users table, even though the referenced table is not present in this node's touch-set.
read_status defaults to an unread state (e.g. boolean false) so newly inserted notifications appear unread.
notification_type is stored as a constrained string/enum rather than free text, given the fixed summary wording.
The schema definition in db/schema/notifications.js is intended to stay in sync with the raw SQL migration as the ORM/source-of-truth mirror.

analysis.text: If sender_id/recipient_id are declared as foreign keys but the referenced users table or migration order is not guaranteed, the CREATE TABLE can fail on a fresh database where the parent table does not yet exist.

Notification queries are typically filtered by recipient_id and read_status; without an index on (recipient_id, read_status) the unread-count and feed queries will degrade to full scans as the table grows.
Migration reversibility is unspecified; if no down/rollback is provided the create cannot be cleanly reverted in a failed deploy, leaving an orphaned table.
Drift risk: the SQL migration and the db/schema/notifications.js definition can diverge (column types, nullability, defaults) since they are maintained as two artifacts of the same table.
content is user-influenced text; if stored without length bounds it permits unbounded payloads, and downstream consumers must treat it as untrusted on render.

benefits.text: Establishes a single backend source of truth for notification persistence that API and UI lanes can build against independently.
Modeling read_status and timestamps at the schema level enables unread-count and chronological feed queries without application-side bookkeeping.
Keeping the change confined to the migration and schema mirror keeps the blast radius isolated from API/UI work, reducing cross-lane coordination.

notable_symbols.why_notable: The DDL that creates the table; defines columns, keys, defaults and any indexes — the authoritative shape applied to the database.
The application-layer schema/model mirror that downstream API code will import; must match the SQL migration exactly to avoid drift.

assumptions.text: The test targets a NotificationSettingsPanel component that renders one toggle per notification type.
The component emits preference changes via a callback prop (e.g. onChange/onPreferenceChange) asserted by the test.
Rendering is exercised with a component testing library (React Testing Library / Jest) consistent with the .test.jsx convention.

analysis.text: Test may only cover the default toggle state and miss the case where all notification types are disabled or a preference value is missing, leaving rendering-of-empty-state unverified.
Asserting on emitted preference changes via a callback can be flaky if the change handler fires asynchronously and the test does not await the update.
Querying toggles by visible label couples the test to copy text; localized or renamed labels would break selection without a stable test id.

Verifies the preference-change emission so downstream consumers of the change event keep receiving correct payloads.

assumptions.text: Both endpoints are wired through notificationsController, which contains the send and list handler logic.
GET /notifications supports pagination and filtering query parameters (e.g. user, limit, offset) per the node summary.
POST /notifications/send persists a notification record to a backing store, though no schema_keys are listed in the touch-set so the persistence layer is not resolved here.
The notifications API is an independent lane and does not modify shared signatures or config (signatures_changed and config_keys are empty).

analysis.text: GET /notifications lists notifications 'for a user' but the touch-set shows no auth or ownership enforcement symbol; without scoping by the authenticated principal, a user could read another user's notifications via a forged user filter.
Pagination/filtering params on GET /notifications need validation (non-numeric limit/offset, negative values, oversized limit). Unbounded limit can return the full table.
POST /notifications/send lacks visible request-body validation in the touch-set; missing required fields (recipient, message) could persist malformed notifications or throw uncaught errors.
A list endpoint without an enforced max page size or indexed filter column can degrade as the notifications volume grows; the persistence/index strategy is unresolved (no schema_keys in touch-set).

benefits.text: Consolidates both write (send) and read (list) notification flows behind a single controller, keeping the API lane self-contained and independently deployable.
Pagination/filtering on GET /notifications lets clients fetch user-scoped slices instead of full result sets, supporting responsive notification UIs.

notable_symbols.why_notable: New write endpoint that stores a notification; entry point for input validation and persistence concerns.
New read endpoint with pagination/filtering; primary surface for authz scoping and query validation.
Holds the handler logic for both endpoints; the single place where validation, auth scoping, and store access converge.
